newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-No Telstra preference shares, Costello says.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-No Telstra preference shares, Costello says.

text.p: Issuing preference shares for Telstra never seemed likely, and Treasurer Peter Costello virtually ruled out the possibility in Question Time on Tuesday.

This leaves us pondering Independent senator Brian Harradine's statement last week that the Telstra (Dilution of Public Ownership) Bill would not get his vote in "the first instance" and might not in the second instance.

The second instance he was talking about was, apparently, a second presentation of the bill to the Senate at least three months after its initial rejection, as specified by the deadlock-breaking mechanism in the Constitution.
Costello's argument was crystal clear: preference shares are a form of financing which would attract interest rates based on Telstra's credit rating.
As creditworthy as Telstra might be, it cannot match the federal government, and the government would be only swapping its cheap debt for expensive debt.

Notably, Costello did not conclusively say that preference shares were definitely not a possibility. Instead, he repeated the formula that it held no attraction to the government, which carries only an implication that it is not on.
But Canberra Watch notes that Costello has a strong politician's habit of avoiding direct statements. So we should not assume that his ambiguity is deliberate.
Here is the core of his statement to the House of Representatives, which followed a question from a government member of parliament:
"That proposal holds no attraction for the government ..."
"It essentially amounts to a financing transaction.
"It essentially would be borrowing off the back of the Telstra security and if the government is to borrow it would prefer to borrow on its own account with its own credit rating.
"The differential would be lower and there would be no basis whatsoever for not being able to raise the required funds in the bond markets with Treasury bonds."

After the usual smack at the Labor Party over public debt levels, he finished with: "In relation to the government's policy, the policy it put to the election, the policy that the Australian people endorsed on the second of March, we will be implementing it."
Harradine has already said in private conversation that he was not happy with Costello's statement.
